props.title: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
props.initialSlug: Mental ward rebel sparks patients' fight for freedom

sections.content: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest revolutionized the portrayal of mental health institutions in cinema through Jack Nicholson's electric performance as R.P. McMurphy, a criminal who fakes insanity to serve his sentence in a psychiatric hospital rather than prison. Director Milos Forman crafted a masterpiece that swept all five major Academy Awards - a feat matched only by It Happened One Night (1934) and The Silence of the Lambs (1991). The film's impact resonates through later institutional critiques like Girl, Interrupted (1999) and Shutter Island (2010), establishing a template for examining power structures and institutional control.

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond mental health narratives into broader examinations of institutional authority and rebellion. Louise Fletcher's portrayal of Nurse Ratched created an archetype of bureaucratic evil that influenced characters like Dolores Umbridge in Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (2007). The ward dynamics and power struggles echo through prison dramas like The Shawshank Redemption (1994) and Cool Hand Luke (1967), where individual spirit clashes with systematic oppression. SUBHEAD: Impact on Mental Health in Cinema

Following Cuckoo's Nest, films began approaching mental health with greater complexity. Awakenings (1990) explored treatment breakthroughs with humanity and nuance, while A Beautiful Mind (2001) depicted schizophrenia from an intimate first-person perspective. The film's influence can be seen in contemporary works like Silver Linings Playbook (2012) and The Perks of Being a Wallflower (2012), which treat mental health challenges with greater empathy and understanding rather than exploitation.
